name: Jinyangjo
desc: The slowest pansori/sanjo jangdan, a stately six-beat gak in compound triple (encoded as 6 beats x 3 = 18), with the changgo kung (low) on the main beats and accented deok strokes marking the lyrical, meditative cycle.

name: Jungmori
desc: A walking-tempo twelve-beat jangdan (12/4) basic to all sanjo schools, used for descriptive and emotional passages; the deok accent on beat 9 (the 'maett�' cadence) is characteristic.

name: Jungjungmori
desc: An exciting twelve-beat compound-quadruple jangdan (12/8, four beats of three) faster than jungmori, used in lively pansori scenes and folk song; deong on each main beat with deok ornaments.

name: Jajinmori
desc: A fast four-beat compound jangdan (12/8) whose basic figure is 'deong-kung-kungdeok-kung'; drives dramatic, urgent sections of pansori, sanjo, nongak and shaman muga.

name: Eotmori
desc: A lopsided, fast 10/8 jangdan grouped 3+2+3+2, used for mysterious or supernatural pansori passages; the asymmetric kung/deok placement gives its distinctive limping swing.

name: Hwimori
desc: The fastest pansori jangdan, four rapid compound beats (also called dangak in shaman music) used when events rush by; a relentless alternation of deong and kung.

name: Danmori
desc: The simple-duple counterpart of hwimori (4/4) closing many sanjo, extremely fast with two sobak per beat; steady deong-kung drive to the finale.

name: Semachi
desc: A bright three-beat folk jangdan (9/8) faster than gutgeori, giving cheerful, valiant feeling; kung opens each of the three compound beats with deok ornaments.

name: Gutgeori
desc: The most common folk jangdan, a twelve-beat compound cycle 'deong-gideok-kung deoreoreoreo / kung-gideok-kung deoreoreoreo', basis of much Korean dance and folk song.

name: Eotjungmori
desc: An asymmetric pansori jangdan in a slow uneven grouping, used for solemn or off-balance narrative passages; the kung articulates the irregular metric divisions.

name: Dongsalpuri
desc: Salpuri-derived shaman/dance jangdan (also called obangjin) in a flowing compound twelve, accompanying ritual and the famous Korean cleansing dance; smooth deong-deoreoreo phrasing.

name: Gukkeori (Gyeonggi gut)
desc: A regional variant of the twelve-beat gutgeori used in Seoul/Gyeonggi gut (shaman ritual), looser and more syncopated than the dance form.

name: Jungmori (slow danga)
desc: The danga (warm-up song) reading of jungmori, three groups of four with the cadential deok on the eleventh beat marking the end of each line of text.

name: Eongmori
desc: A rare wide 14-beat pansori jangdan (grouped unevenly) used for grand or expansive scenes; the kung anchors the two large halves while deok marks the inner subdivisions.

name: Samul nori Binari
desc: The blessing-chant opening of a samul nori program; a moderate compound twelve where janggu and buk lay a steady deong-kung bed under the kkwaenggwari invocation.

name: Samdo Nongak (Binari-gut)
desc: From the seated 'three-provinces farmers' band' suite; a driving four-beat compound groove with the deong on the main beats answered by off-beat deok strokes and dense deoreoreo rolls.

name: Yeongnam Nongak (Gilgunak)
desc: The processional 'road' rhythm of the Yeongnam (southeast) nongak suite; a marching pulse adapted for samul nori with kung on the three big beats and syncopated deok strokes.

name: Yeongnam Byeoldalgeori
desc: A syncopated section of the Yeongnam nongak suite famous in samul nori for its off-beat kkwaenggwari calls answered by displaced janggu deong accents.

name: Samdo Seoltjanggu (Dadeuraegi)
desc: From the virtuoso four-janggu showpiece of the 'three provinces'; intricate interlocking deong/deok/gideok figures showcasing the changgo's two-hand technique.

name: Hwimori (samul nori finale)
desc: The accelerating climactic hwimori that ends most samul nori performances; near-continuous deong-deok hammering over four compound beats building to the unison stop.

name: Pungmul Samchae
desc: The 'three-stroke' farmers'-band pattern (samchae) of pungmul nori, a three-beat compound cycle that propels the dancing procession with buk on the down-beats.

name: Matsuri Don-doko
desc: The basic festival 'don-doko-don-doko' nagado-daiko ground beat under matsuri-bayashi, with the low don on the beats and doko fills between, shime-daiko keeping the ji-uchi.

name: Miyake (Kiyari-daiko)
desc: The low, wide-stance Miyake-jima style from the Gozu Tenno festival; a powerful syncopated 'do-don, do-do-don' phrase struck on the side-mounted nagado-daiko.

name: Yatai-bayashi
desc: The fast Chichibu float-festival piece famous for its relentless 'doko-doko' sixteenth stream and seated, leaning posture; the low taiko drives a near-continuous roll.

name: Hachijo-daiko
desc: The Hachijo-jima two-player tradition where a fixed shita-byoshi underbeat supports a free improvised upper part; this encodes a typical bouncing shita-byoshi don-pattern.

name: Bon Odori Ondo
desc: The swinging duple ondo groove for Bon-odori circle dancing; low taiko on the down-beats with the kane/shime back-beat accents that carry the singer's call-and-response.

name: Tanko-bushi
desc: The 'coal-miner's song', Japan's most popular Bon-odori min'yo; a clean two-beat ondo feel with the taiko marking the digging-and-tossing dance gestures.

name: Soran-bushi
desc: The Hokkaido herring-fishers' work song; a vigorous duple net-hauling rhythm with strong low taiko on every half-beat under the 'yaren soran' shouts.

name: Shishimai (lion dance)
desc: Accompaniment for the Japanese shishi (lion) dance with flute and shime; an irregular, prowling taiko figure that cues the lion's lunges and head shakes.

name: Gion-bayashi
desc: The kane-and-flute 'kon-chiki-chin' float music of Kyoto's Gion Matsuri; a steady gong ostinato over a light taiko pulse leading the yamaboko procession.

name: Edo-bayashi
desc: Tokyo festival ensemble music with two shime, one nagado-daiko, kane and flute; interlocking on-beat taiko and off-beat shime create its busy festival drive.

name: Jiuchi Don-doko (base beat)
desc: The foundational ji-uchi 'don (su) doko' pulse that underlies most kumi-daiko pieces, supplying the steady metric bed over which solo phrases are played.

name: Yagura-bayashi
desc: Drumming from atop the Bon-odori yagura tower; a lilting syncopated taiko call that the encircling dancers follow, alternating low don with rim ka accents.

name: Nokorigaku Yo-hyoshi
desc: A four-kobyoshi (yo-hyoshi) gagaku cycle: the great taiko marks the start of each four-beat unit while the kakko fills with rolls and the shoko strikes the back-beats.

name: Gagaku Ya-hyoshi (eight-beat)
desc: The eight-kobyoshi ya-hyoshi gagaku pattern of kangen music; the slow taiko stroke crowns the long cycle, kakko anticipates with katarai rolls and shoko marks midpoints.

name: Gagaku Tadabyoshi
desc: The standard tadabyoshi metric frame of togaku where taiko and kakko coordinate the colotomic cycle, the shoko gong filling the off-beats of the courtly tempo.

name: Jingju Sigexiang
desc: A core Peking-opera entrance pattern ('si ji tou' family) where danpigu drum, daluo, naobo cymbals and xiaoluo interlock as 'cang-qi-cang' to set up an actor's appearance.

name: Jingju Jijifeng
desc: The 'fast wind' battle pattern (jijifeng) of jingju, an accelerating continuous gong-and-drum tremolo accompanying fights and frantic action on the Peking-opera stage.

name: Jingju Manchangchui
desc: A stately slow gong pattern of Peking opera used for dignified entrances and aria introductions; the daluo's falling pitch on the strong beats conveys solemnity.

name: Luogu Ba Da Cang
desc: The classic 'du... ba-da-cang' cadential gong-drum figure that punctuates stage action, the gu drum rolling into the cymbal-and-gong 'cang' downstroke.

name: Luogu Beng-deng-cang
desc: The short 'beng-deng-cang' emphasis figure marking an actor's movement or pose, two drum taps resolving onto the gong-cymbal 'cang'.

name: Lion Dance Sam Sing (three-star)
desc: The 'three-star' (saam sing) lion-dance drum call, three big drum-gong-cymbal hits that signal the lion to bow or salute before the main routine.

name: Lion Dance Cai Qing (marching)
desc: The walking/seven-star drum groove driving a lion's approach to the cai-qing ('plucking the greens') challenge, steady drum with cymbal-and-gong on the strong beats.

name: Jiangnan Sizhu Lao Liuban
desc: The 'Old Six-Beat' (Lao Liuban / Baban) stock tune of Jiangnan silk-and-bamboo music; the ban clapper and gu drum frame the eight-bar 'eight-beat' metric skeleton.

name: Ba Ban (Eight Beats)
desc: The ubiquitous 'Baban' eight-beat tune-skeleton underlying countless Chinese folk and opera pieces; the ban marks each beat (banyan) with a strong-beat accent structure.

name: Chaozhou Luogu
desc: The drum-gong style of Chaozhou (eastern Guangdong), led by the daluo gong-drum (da luogu) with bright cymbal interplay over a steady duple drum pulse.

name: Cantonese Lion Drum (Qixing)
desc: The Cantonese 'seven-star' (cat sing) lion-dance drum cadence with its characteristic syncopated drum roll into the gong-cymbal answer, used between dance figures.

name: Yangge (rice-sprout dance)
desc: The northern-Chinese yangge folk-dance groove driven by waist-drum and gong; a bouncy duple 'cang-cang' beat for the swaying processional rice-planting dance.

name: Yanggao Ritual Drum
desc: A drum pattern from the Yanggao (Shanxi) ritual shawm-band tradition, where drum and cymbals punctuate the suona melody with irregular accented strokes.

name: Okinawan Eisa
desc: The Okinawan Bon dance drumming for the ancestral spirits, with the large odaiko on the down-beats and shime/paranku frame-drums dancing the marching duple groove.

name: Okinawan Kachashi
desc: The fast, joyous Okinawan kachashi celebration rhythm danced with raised hands; a quick uptempo duple driven by sanshin, taiko and clapping at weddings and parties.

name: Mongolian Long-song Drum
desc: A spacious compound frame-drum pulse evoking Mongolian pastoral song and shamanic rite; broad low strokes with rolling fills under the wide melodic phrases.

name: Mongolian Shaman Frame Drum
desc: The steady hypnotic frame-drum (tsetsuukhei) pulse of Mongolian/Buryat shamanic ritual, an even galloping beat sustaining trance and invocation.

name: Tuvan Horse-gait Groove
desc: An imitative 'horse-gait' rhythm pervasive in Tuvan throat-singing music, the paired low strokes evoking a galloping or ambling horse beneath the khoomei drone.

name: Tuvan Igil Trot
desc: A brisk trotting pulse that underlies igil-and-doshpuluur dance tunes in Tuva, a clean duple that mirrors the steady gait of the steppe horse.

name: Sword/Spear Dance (Jianqi)
desc: A martial gong-drum pattern accompanying weapon-dance and acrobatic combat scenes in Chinese opera, the cymbals slashing off-beats around the drum's strong strokes.

name: Liangping Laizi Luogu
desc: The 'laizi' gong-drum suite of Liangping (Chongqing), a lively folk percussion ensemble pattern of interlocking small-gong and drum heard at village festivals.
